title: Best Hangover Prevention Drinks: What to Drink Before Alcohol
excerpt: Which drinks actually help prevent a hangover? An honest ranking of water, electrolytes, DHM, ZBiotics, pear juice and hangover shots, with what to drink before, during and after.
metaDescription: Which hangover prevention drinks work? An honest ranking of electrolytes, DHM, ZBiotics, pear juice and hangover shots, plus what to drink before alcohol.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** no drink you can buy will reliably stop a hangover if you drink a lot. The things that help most are free and boring: eating a real meal before you start, alternating each alcoholic drink with a glass of water, choosing lighter drinks, and simply drinking less. "Hangover prevention drinks" sit on top of those habits. The best of them make a modest difference for some people; the worst are expensive sugar water with a confident label.

**Our quick picks:** For most people, the best pre-drinking drink is plain water plus a salty meal. If you want a product, a sugar-light electrolyte drink before bed covers hydration, and a DHM-based product such as [Cheers Restore](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B079P7FXTW?tag=dhmguide-20) is the option we think has the most interesting research behind it, with the caveat that the human evidence is still thin. ZBiotics, a pre-drinking probiotic, has a clever idea behind it but mostly company-funded data. We explain each one below, including what it actually does, who it suits, and where the marketing runs ahead of the science.

> **Safety first.** This article is general information, not medical advice. No drink or supplement lowers your blood alcohol level or makes it safe to drive, and none protects you from alcohol poisoning. Check with a doctor or pharmacist before using supplements if you're pregnant, take prescription medicine (especially blood thinners, diabetes medicine, sedatives, or anything metabolized by the liver), or have liver or kidney disease. **Call 911 (or your local emergency number) if someone who has been drinking** can't be woken, has slow or irregular breathing, has blue-tinged or cold, clammy skin, has a seizure, or is vomiting while barely conscious. Don't leave them alone to "sleep it off."

## What a Hangover Prevention Drink Can and Can't Do

To judge any product, it helps to know what actually causes a hangover. Researchers still argue about the details, but the main contributors are fairly well established:

- **Alcohol itself and how much you drank.** This is by far the biggest factor. Higher peak blood alcohol and more total drinks mean worse hangovers.
- **Acetaldehyde.** Your liver turns alcohol into acetaldehyde, a toxic compound, before breaking it down further. How much it contributes to next-day symptoms is debated, but it's the target of several products.
- **Inflammation and immune signaling.** Heavy drinking triggers an inflammatory response, and hangover severity tracks with some of those markers in studies.
- **Poor sleep.** Alcohol helps you fall asleep but fragments sleep in the second half of the night.
- **Fluid loss.** Alcohol suppresses vasopressin (the hormone that tells your kidneys to hold onto water), so you pee more. You can read more in our guide to [whether to take electrolytes before or after drinking](/never-hungover/electrolytes-before-or-after-drinking).
- **Congeners.** These are by-products of fermentation and aging, found in higher amounts in darker drinks like bourbon, brandy, and red wine. A well-known study by Rohsenow and colleagues found bourbon produced worse hangovers than vodka at the same blood alcohol level. See our explainer on [congeners in alcohol](/never-hungover/congeners-in-alcohol).
- **Low blood sugar and an irritated stomach**, especially if you drank without eating.

Here's the key point. Dehydration is the cause most drinks are marketed around, yet hangover researchers have found that markers of dehydration only loosely track how bad people feel the next day. Fixing fluids is worth doing because it helps with thirst, dry mouth, and headache. It just isn't the whole story, which is why a hydration drink alone rarely prevents a hangover after a heavy night.

So a realistic goal for any pre-drinking drink is to **trim** symptoms, not to cancel them. If a product promises you'll wake up feeling like you never drank, treat that as a red flag.

## How We Judged These Drinks

We looked at four things for each option:

1. **Plausible mechanism.** Does it target something that actually contributes to hangovers?
2. **Quality of evidence.** Are there independent human studies, or only animal data and company claims?
3. **Cost and convenience.** Price per night and whether you'll actually use it.
4. **Downsides.** Sugar, side effects, interactions, and whether it encourages drinking more.

We haven't run our own clinical trials, and we say so plainly where the evidence is weak. Brands are listed for comparison. We only link to stores for products we carry.

## The Best Hangover Prevention Drinks, Ranked

### 1. Water and a real meal (the free baseline)

Before you spend money, get the basics right. Drinking a glass of water between alcoholic drinks slows your pace and keeps fluid intake up. Eating a meal with protein, fat, and fiber before drinking slows how quickly alcohol moves from your stomach into your small intestine, where most of it is absorbed. That lowers your peak blood alcohol, which is one of the strongest predictors of how you'll feel tomorrow. Our guides on [what to eat before drinking](/never-hungover/what-to-eat-before-drinking-alcohol-evidence-based-guide) and [drinking on an empty stomach](/never-hungover/drinking-on-an-empty-stomach) go into detail.

- **Pros:** Free, no side effects, backed by basic physiology.
- **Cons:** Requires discipline at the bar, which is harder than opening a packet.
- **Best for:** Everyone, every time. Every product below works better on top of this.

### 2. DHM drinks and supplements (most promising research)

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a compound from the Japanese raisin tree (*Hovenia dulcis*), used in traditional East Asian hangover remedies. A widely cited 2012 study in the *Journal of Neuroscience* by Shen and colleagues found DHM reduced alcohol intoxication and withdrawal-like effects in rats, apparently by acting on GABA-A receptors in the brain, the same receptors alcohol acts on. Other lab and animal work suggests DHM may support the enzymes that clear alcohol and acetaldehyde and may reduce alcohol-related liver stress.

The honest caveat: most of that work is in animals and cells. Human data is limited, and there is no good evidence that DHM prevents hangovers in everyone or lets you drink more safely. We go through the studies in detail in [Does DHM actually work?](/never-hungover/does-dhm-work-honest-science-review-2025)

DHM comes in a few forms:

- **Capsules taken with your drinks or before bed.** These are the cheapest per night and the easiest to carry. Popular picks include [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) for value and [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), which adds L-cysteine and electrolytes.
- **Multi-ingredient "recovery" formulas** like [Cheers Restore](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B079P7FXTW?tag=dhmguide-20) and [Flyby Recovery](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0CCK34H46?tag=dhmguide-20), which pair DHM with vitamins, milk thistle, or other ingredients. See our full [Cheers Restore review](/never-hungover/cheers-restore-review) and [Flyby review](/never-hungover/flyby-recovery-review-2025).
- **Ready-to-drink shots.** Some brands sell DHM in a small bottle you drink during or after a night out. These are convenient but usually cost more per serving than capsules.

**Pros:** The most interesting mechanism of any option here, generally well tolerated in studies, inexpensive in capsule form.
**Cons:** Limited human research, dosing varies a lot between brands, and it's still a supplement, so quality depends on the maker.
**Best for:** People who drink occasionally and want something beyond water and electrolytes. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much and when.

### 3. Electrolyte drinks (best for hydration, not a cure)

Electrolyte drinks contain sodium, potassium, and usually some sugar, which helps your gut absorb water faster than plain water alone. That's the principle behind oral rehydration solutions used for diarrhea. Popular options include Liquid I.V., Pedialyte, DripDrop, LMNT, and Ultima Replenisher. We compare them in our [best electrolyte drink for a hangover](/never-hungover/electrolyte-drinks-for-hangover-compared) guide.

When to drink them matters more than which brand you pick. A serving before you go out does little, because you'll pee much of it out once the alcohol kicks in. The more useful moments are **one serving before bed** and **another when you wake up**, especially if you were sweating on a dance floor or vomited.

- **Pros:** Easy, cheap per serving, genuinely helps thirst and dry mouth, useful if you've been sweating or vomiting.
- **Cons:** Doesn't touch acetaldehyde, inflammation, or sleep. Some formulas carry a fair amount of sugar, and high-sodium options aren't ideal if you've been told to limit salt.
- **Best for:** Hot weather, long nights, dancing, and anyone who reliably wakes up parched.

### 4. ZBiotics (clever idea, thin independent evidence)

ZBiotics is a genetically engineered probiotic (a strain of *Bacillus subtilis*) designed to produce an enzyme that breaks down acetaldehyde in your gut. You drink one small bottle before your first drink.

The idea is creative, but there are two open questions. Most acetaldehyde is made in the liver, not the gut, so it's unclear how much a gut-based enzyme can do. And the supporting data comes mainly from the company itself rather than large independent trials. Plenty of users report a difference; plenty report none. Our [ZBiotics review](/never-hungover/zbiotics-review) and [DHM vs ZBiotics comparison](/never-hungover/dhm-vs-zbiotics) cover it in depth.

- **Pros:** Single serving taken once, no known safety concerns for healthy adults, genuinely novel approach.
- **Cons:** Expensive per night, mostly company-funded evidence, doesn't address hydration or sleep.
- **Best for:** People who are curious and for whom price isn't a concern. We don't carry it, so we don't link to a store.

### 5. Coconut water (a gentle natural option)

Coconut water is naturally high in potassium and contains some sugar and a modest amount of sodium. It's lower in sodium than a proper oral rehydration drink, so it's better as a pleasant morning drink than a serious rehydration tool. Details are in our [coconut water for hangover](/never-hungover/coconut-water-for-hangover) guide.

- **Pros:** Natural, easy on the stomach, tastes good to many people.
- **Cons:** Low sodium compared with electrolyte drinks, calories add up, and it doesn't do anything special to prevent a hangover.
- **Best for:** People who dislike the taste of electrolyte powders.

### 6. Korean pear juice (small but real study)

Asian pear juice is a traditional Korean remedy, and it's one of the few foods tested specifically as a drink *before* alcohol. A small study by Australia's national science agency, CSIRO, reported in 2013 that drinking about 220 ml of Korean pear juice before alcohol was linked to lower ratings on some hangover symptoms. The study was small and has not been widely replicated, so treat it as interesting rather than settled.

- **Pros:** Cheap, food-based, low risk.
- **Cons:** Limited evidence, needs to be the Korean (Asian) pear variety, and the effect, if any, is modest.
- **Best for:** People who'd rather try a food than a supplement.

### 7. Milk or a protein shake (old trick, partly true)

The idea that milk "lines your stomach" isn't quite right; it doesn't coat anything. What it does do is put food in your stomach, which slows alcohol absorption just like any meal. A glass of milk or a protein shake is better than nothing if you can't eat a proper dinner. It isn't better than a proper dinner.

- **Pros:** Easy, slows absorption a bit, cheap.
- **Cons:** No special effect beyond being food; dairy doesn't suit everyone.
- **Best for:** When you're heading out straight from work and can't sit down to eat.

### 8. Multivitamin and "detox" drinks (mostly marketing)

A wide range of products such as vitamin-packed shots, B-vitamin drinks, and branded "pre-party" formulas are sold for hangover prevention. Some contain reasonable ingredients like B vitamins, vitamin C, or N-acetylcysteine (NAC). The problem is that very few have been tested as finished products in people, and B vitamins can't make up for the effects of heavy drinking in one night. Our reviews of [Drinkwel](/never-hungover/drinkwel-review) and [H-Proof](/never-hungover/h-proof-review) show how this plays out with specific brands.

- **Pros:** Usually harmless, sometimes useful if your diet is poor.
- **Cons:** Big claims, little product-specific evidence, often pricey.
- **Best for:** Skip unless you have a specific reason.

## Drinks to Avoid Before and During a Night Out

Some of the worst hangover decisions happen in the glass, not the medicine cabinet.

- **Energy drinks mixed with alcohol.** Caffeine masks how drunk you feel, which tends to make people drink more. Health agencies, including the CDC, have warned about this combination.
- **Sugary, carbonated mixers.** Carbonation may speed how quickly alcohol enters your bloodstream, and some small studies have found diet mixers lead to higher breath alcohol than sugary ones because the stomach empties faster. Either way, a fizzy mixer won't protect you. What matters most is how much alcohol is in the glass.
- **Dark spirits and red wine in large amounts**, because of their higher congener content. If you're prone to bad hangovers, clearer drinks are a reasonable choice. Our ranking of the [least hangover-prone alcohol](/never-hungover/least-hangover-alcohol-ranked) explains why.
- **Shots in quick succession.** These drive a sharp spike in blood alcohol, which is exactly what you're trying to avoid.

And one myth to drop: the order of drinks doesn't matter much. Research testing "beer before wine" found that total alcohol drives the hangover, not the sequence. We cover it in [beer before liquor: myth or fact?](/never-hungover/beer-before-liquor-myth)

## What to Drink Before Drinking Alcohol: A Simple Plan

If you want one routine to follow, here it is:

1. **Two to three hours before:** Eat a full meal with protein, fat, and complex carbs. Drink a large glass of water.
2. **Right before you start:** If you use a supplement like DHM, many people take it now or with their first drink. Follow the label. If you use ZBiotics, this is when the company says to take it.
3. **During the night:** One glass of water for every alcoholic drink. Choose lighter drinks and set a number before you start.
4. **Before bed:** A glass of water or an electrolyte drink. Some DHM users take a second dose at this point; again, follow the label.
5. **In the morning:** More water or an electrolyte drink, a gentle breakfast, and rest. Our list of [the best hangover recovery drinks](/never-hungover/best-hangover-recovery-drinks) covers the morning-after side.

None of these steps is dramatic on its own. Together, they make a real difference for most social drinkers.

## Hangover Prevention Shots: Worth It?

"Hangover shots" are small bottles, usually 50 to 100 ml, taken before, during, or after drinking. They're popular in South Korea, where convenience stores sell many brands, and they've spread to the US. Ingredient lists vary widely: some contain DHM or *Hovenia dulcis* extract, others rely on ginseng, herbal extracts, vitamins, or electrolytes.

Whether one is worth buying depends on what's inside. A shot built around a meaningful dose of DHM is in roughly the same evidence category as DHM capsules, just pricier per serving. A shot that's mostly sugar, flavoring, and a pinch of vitamins is mostly marketing. Read the label: look for the actual amount of each active ingredient rather than a "proprietary blend" that hides the doses.

## Does Pedialyte Before Drinking Prevent a Hangover?

Pedialyte is a well-designed oral rehydration solution, and it helps if you're already dehydrated. Drinking it *before* you go out, though, does little to prevent a hangover, because alcohol makes your kidneys release water no matter how well hydrated you started. You'll get more value drinking it before bed and the next morning. If you're comparing it with sports drinks, see our [Pedialyte vs Gatorade](/never-hungover/pedialyte-vs-gatorade-hangover) breakdown.

## Who Should Be Careful With Prevention Products

Most of these drinks are low-risk for healthy adults, but a few groups should check with a doctor or pharmacist first:

- **People on prescription medicine**, especially blood thinners, diabetes medicine, sedatives, antidepressants, or drugs processed by the liver. Supplements can interact, and alcohol already interacts with many of these. Our [DHM and medication interactions](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) guide has more.
- **People with kidney disease or heart failure**, who may need to limit sodium and potassium in electrolyte drinks.
- **People with diabetes**, because both sugary drinks and alcohol affect blood sugar, and alcohol can cause delayed low blood sugar.
- **Anyone pregnant or breastfeeding**, where no amount of alcohol is considered safe.

It's also worth being honest about one risk: if a product makes you feel "protected," it's easy to drink more than you otherwise would. That trade usually ends badly. Use prevention products to take the edge off a normal night, not to stretch it.

## When to See a Doctor

Hangovers are miserable but normally pass within a day. Get medical help if you notice:

- Vomiting that won't stop, or you can't keep any fluids down for many hours.
- Confusion, severe drowsiness, or trouble staying awake.
- Chest pain, a racing or irregular heartbeat, or trouble breathing.
- Shaking, sweating, anxiety, or a racing heart that shows up when you *stop* drinking after several days of heavy drinking. These can be signs of alcohol withdrawal, which can become dangerous and needs medical care.
- Yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, or pain under the right ribs.

If you find you regularly need a prevention routine to get through the week, it's worth talking to your doctor about your drinking. That's a health check, not a judgment.

## The Bottom Line

The best hangover prevention drink is a glass of water, taken often, after a proper meal. Electrolyte drinks are worth having before bed and in the morning, especially after a sweaty night. Among supplements, DHM has the most interesting research, mainly in animals, and is a reasonable thing to try alongside good habits. ZBiotics, pear juice, and hangover shots are optional experiments with limited evidence. Nothing in a bottle replaces drinking less, and nothing makes it safe to drive.

If you want to try DHM, start with a well-reviewed, clearly dosed product such as [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) or [Cheers Restore](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B079P7FXTW?tag=dhmguide-20), and read our full guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) for the habits that do most of the work.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the best drink to prevent a hangover?**

Plain water, taken between alcoholic drinks, after a proper meal, is the best-supported option and it's free. If you want a product, an electrolyte drink before bed and in the morning helps with thirst and dry mouth, and DHM-based supplements have promising, mostly animal research. No drink reliably prevents a hangover after heavy drinking.

**What should I drink before drinking alcohol?**

A large glass of water with a full meal two to three hours before is the most useful start. Milk or a protein shake helps a little if you can't eat, because any food slows alcohol absorption. If you use a supplement like DHM or a product like ZBiotics, follow the label on timing. Avoid energy drinks, which mask how drunk you feel.

**Do hangover prevention shots work?**

It depends on what's in them. Shots with a meaningful dose of DHM or Hovenia dulcis extract are in the same evidence category as DHM capsules: promising but limited human research. Shots made mostly of sugar, flavoring, and a few vitamins have little evidence behind them. Check the label for actual ingredient amounts rather than a proprietary blend.

**Does drinking electrolytes before drinking prevent a hangover?**

Not much. Alcohol makes your kidneys release water no matter how hydrated you start, so a pre-party electrolyte drink is mostly lost. Electrolytes are more useful before bed and the next morning. Even then they help with thirst, dry mouth, and headache rather than preventing the hangover itself, because dehydration is only one part of what causes it.

**Does ZBiotics prevent hangovers?**

There is no good independent evidence that ZBiotics prevents hangovers for most people. It's an engineered probiotic designed to break down acetaldehyde in the gut, which is a clever idea, but most acetaldehyde is made in the liver and the supporting data comes mainly from the company. It appears safe for healthy adults, so it's a reasonable experiment if the price doesn't bother you.

**Is DHM better than electrolyte drinks for hangovers?**

They do different jobs. Electrolyte drinks replace fluid and salts, which helps thirst and dry mouth. DHM targets how the body and brain respond to alcohol, with research mostly from animal studies. Many people use both: DHM with their drinks or before bed, and an electrolyte drink before bed and in the morning, on top of water and food.

**Can a drink stop me from getting drunk?**

No. No drink or supplement lowers your blood alcohol level enough to make you sober or safe to drive. Food slows absorption and water slows your pace, which helps, but the only reliable way to be less drunk is to drink less alcohol. Never rely on a prevention product before driving.
